LOSS OF LIFE FOLLOWING MAN OVERBOARD FROM P/V QUEEN OF THE WEST
2) Violation of Safety Policies: American Cruise Lines, Inc. had several safety policies in
place that could have effectively prevented this incident if Mr. Staples had been
following them. Mr. Staples was made aware of the policies when he signed on to work
as a galley steward. Had Mr. Staples abided by the "Crew in Quarters after Midnight"
policy, he would have been in his berth instead of on the stern. Furthermore, had he been
following the "No Smoking" policy, he would have gone to shore to smoke instead of
placing himself in a hazardous area of the vessel. Finally, Mr. Staples violated the "No
Alcohol"policy by consuming alcohol earlier that night.
3) Fatigue: Historically, marine casualty investigations have shown that fatigue often
contributes to errors in judgment and attention failures. In this case, it cannot be
conclusively determined if fatigue was a factor in Mr. Staples' fall overboard, but the
likelihood that Mr. Staples was suffering from fatigue is high. At the end of his shift, he

to the vessel, where he stayed up playing video games with other off-duty crew. He fell
overboard shortly after 0100 hrs. "Al three witnesses saw him slip on the step when he
approached the paddlewheel, one witness saw him slip twice. He was also observed to
fumble with clutching at the paddlewheel boards before falling off the vessel. Although
witnesses were unable to tell investigators exactly how long Mr. Staples had been awake,
it can be safely inferred through witness statements that fatigue played a role in his fall
overboard.
Safety Equipment:
e)
1) Deck Lighting: Although witnesses conflicted as to whether the flood light was on at the
time of the incident, the fact that the light was wired on a separate switch from the rest of
the deck lights allowed investigators to reasonably conclude that the light was likely off
at the time of the fall. Additionally, by leaving the switch in the "off' position, a certain
degree of concealment at night is afforded to unauthorized persons wishing to remain
unseen by vessel managers and passengers. Although witnesses were able to see Mr.
Staples in the water clearly enough to know that his eyes were open and that he was
moving his arms in the water, bright lights flooded the area from the grain facility across
the river which may have provided an extra degree of illumination. But had the light
definitively been in operation, Mr. Staples may have had enough illumination to see his
surroundings, and a fall could have been avoided.
